title: Boss: ship it with evidence
brief: An interviewer asks you to build an evaluation strategy for an AI assistant, before launch and after. Every dial is unspecified. Practise the five steps of Dial-and-Defend out loud, then compare with the model answer.

blocks.text: Open with the dials, not the tools

blocks.title: The interviewer's prompt
known: A new assistant retrieves documents and calls a few tools
It is about to launch, and you must design its evaluation before and after launch
You are expected to compare options and defend a choice
ask: What can go wrong, and how bad is it: a wrong answer, a data leak or an unwanted action?
Which stages exist (retrieval, tools, generation), and do relevance labels or reference answers exist?
Is there any production traffic or trace history, and how many expert hours are available?
How much traffic is expected, and what is the cost ceiling for judge and inference calls?
How fast can a bad release be stopped, and which platform features are preview?
blocks.tension: A heavy pre-launch gate delays the launch and costs expert time. A light gate ships risk. Online scoring catches drift, but only after users saw the answer.

steps.title: Clarify
steps.md: Harm, stages, labels, traffic, expert time, budget, rollback speed.

steps.title: List options
steps.md: Heavy gate, light gate with online scoring, and the layered plan. Name the boring one.

steps.title: Pick and flip
steps.md: Choose for the stated dials. Say what would move you to another plan.

steps.title: Failure modes
steps.md: Judge bias, stale set, noisy gate, contamination, false positives. Say how you detect each.

steps.title: Metrics and rollout
steps.md: Name the numbers you report and the order of release.

blocks.caption: A layered plan across the lifecycle

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.md: They want to hear that you separate retrieval from generation, calibrate the judge, quantify noise with intervals and repeated trials, and label preview features with a fallback. Naming a tool before asking about risk is the most common way to lose the room.

quiz.q: An assistant with retrieval and three tools launches in four weeks. Harm from a wrong action is high, 12 golden cases exist and an expert has two days. Which pre-launch plan gives the most signal for that time?
options: Rerun the existing 12 cases ten times and report the average score, since repetition removes the need for new cases
Grow to about 40 cases with reviewed synthetic rows, score stages separately, and calibrate a pass/fail judge
Adopt a public agent benchmark as the release gate, because it has thousands of tasks and is already labelled
Ship to 5% of users and judge by thumbs ratings, because real traffic is always better than curated test cases
quiz.explain: Starting sets of 20 to 50 cases from real failures, a reviewed synthetic batch for coverage, stage-level scores and a calibrated judge use two expert days well [[r17]] [[r8]]. Repeating 12 cases lowers sampling noise but adds no coverage. A public benchmark does not test your tools or data and can be saturated or contaminated. A 5% launch with thumbs ratings exposes users to high harm and gives a biased signal.

quiz.q: Select every event that should trigger a re-check of the evaluation setup.
options: The agent's system prompt or instructions change materially
The judge model is upgraded or replaced
The retriever's chunking changes, so relevance labels keyed to chunk ids no longer match
The dashboard theme is switched from light to dark
quiz.explain: A synthetic dataset made from one version of the instructions goes stale when they change, so regenerate and version it [[r8]]. A different judge model has different habits, so recalibrate its true positive and true negative rates against the human sample [[r16]]. Labels keyed to old chunk ids score the wrong chunks after a re-chunk. A theme change touches no evaluation input.

quiz.q: Which explanation is best supported, and what is the first action?

code.code:
offline regression suite:     97% pass
sampled online judge score:   falling for 2 weeks
new product feature shipped:  3 weeks ago

options: The online judge is miscalibrated, so the 97% offline pass rate should be trusted instead
The offline suite is too small to mean anything, so its 97% pass rate carries no information
The model provider silently degraded quality, which breaks the service agreement
The golden set no longer covers the new feature's queries, so mine failing traces into it
quiz.explain: The decline began after a feature changed what users ask, which points to a golden set that stopped matching real queries. The first action is to sample the failing traces, confirm with a human-labelled sample that the judge agrees, and add the cases to the set [[r1]]. Ignoring the online judge skips that check. A small suite can still be informative for the cases it covers. A provider regression is possible but nothing in the data points to it.

quiz.q: Match each situation to the evaluation layer that fits it best.

pairs.l: Block a prompt change that breaks citations
pairs.r: CI gate on a regression suite

pairs.l: Detect drift in live answer quality without labels
pairs.r: Continuous evaluation with sampled reference-free judges

pairs.l: Probe for indirect prompt injection before release
pairs.r: Automated red team scan plus expert review

pairs.l: Compare a new model on real requests with no user exposure

quiz.explain: A regression suite with a baseline comparison blocks a known behaviour from breaking. Live traces have no references, so drift needs reference-free judges on a sample. Injection probing needs attacks, which automated scans supply and experts review. Only mirrored traffic lets a candidate see real requests without users seeing its answers.

defend.prompt: We are about to launch an AI assistant that retrieves company documents and calls a few tools. How will you evaluate it before launch and after? Walk me through your options.
clarify: What can go wrong and how bad is it: a wrong answer, a data leak or an unwanted action? That sets the risk tier.
Which stages exist (retrieval, tools, generation), and do relevance labels or reference answers exist?
Is there any production traffic or trace history yet, and how many expert hours are available?
How much traffic will it get, and what is the cost ceiling for judge and inference calls?
How quickly can a bad release be stopped, and which platform features I would rely on are preview?

options.name: Heavy pre-launch gate
options.when: Harm is high, traffic is unknown and rollback is slow.
options.tradeoff: The strongest protection before exposure, but it delays launch, spends scarce expert time and a frozen set drifts from real users.

options.name: Light gate plus online scoring
options.when: Harm is low, errors are cheap to undo, traffic is large and a calibrated judge exists.
options.tradeoff: Fast and realistic, but users see problems first and reference-free judges can mislead.

options.name: Layered: gate, shadow, then sampled scoring
options.when: Most real systems: moderate to high harm, mixed stages and some traffic after a soft launch.
options.tradeoff: The most parts to maintain, and several Foundry features are preview, so it needs a code-first fallback.

modelAnswer.md: **Clarify.** I would first ask what can go wrong and how bad it is, which stages exist, what labels and traces I have, how many expert hours and how much budget there are, and how fast I can stop a bad release. Those are my dials.

**Options and pick.** There are three plans: a heavy pre-launch gate, a light gate with online scoring, and a layered plan. For a system with retrieval and tools and moderate to high harm I would choose the layered plan. Here is what it contains.

items: Golden set: 20 to 50 cases from real failures plus a reviewed synthetic batch. Version it, tag each row by origin and hold out a slice nobody tunes on.
Stage scores: retrieval with rank or judged context metrics at the k the prompt uses, answers with groundedness and completeness, tools with outcome checks plus selected process evaluators.

Judge: one accountable expert labels a sample with critiques. I report true positive and true negative rates, swap order for pairwise, use references where answers are checkable and use a different model family from the generator.
Noise: repeated trials on agent tasks, pass^k and confidence intervals, with the suite sized for the effect I need to see.
Red team: automated scans (preview) plus expert review in a purple environment, including indirect injection.
Gate: a small suite per pull request, a full suite nightly, baseline comparison with significance, blocking on safety and regression suites and advisory capability suites.

Release and after: shadow first when harm is high, then canary, then sampled continuous scoring with caps, scheduled evaluation for drift, feedback as triage and failing traces back into the golden set.

modelAnswer.title: Failure modes and how I detect them
modelAnswer.md: Judge bias shows as swapped-order disagreement and low TNR on a fresh human sample. A stale golden set shows as a widening gap between offline and online scores. A noisy gate shows as run-to-run variance on the same commit. Contamination shows as a held-out slice scoring below the tuned set. Red team false positives show up in manual review.

modelAnswer.caption: What would flip the plan
head: Dial change
Flip to
rows: Harm is very high and rollback is slow
Heavy gate with a named human sign-off before any exposure
No budget for expert labels
Judged context metrics and a panel judge, with the weaker evidence stated
Traffic too low for an A/B test
Shadow runs and paired offline comparisons instead
A needed Foundry feature is preview
A code-first harness as the fallback, with the date of the last check

modelAnswer.md: **Metrics and rollout.** I report recall at k or nDCG, groundedness and completeness, pass^k with intervals, judge TPR and TNR, ASR trend, online score drift and cost per run. Rollout goes from a staff soft launch to shadow, canary and full release, with a rollback trigger tied to a safety evaluator.

rubric.pt: Asks about harm, stages, labels, traffic, expert time and budget before naming tools
Offers at least two plans and picks one for the stated dials
Scores retrieval and generation separately, with k tied to what the prompt receives
Calibrates the judge against an expert and names position, verbosity and self-preference bias
Handles non-determinism with repeated trials, pass^k and confidence intervals
Designs the CI gate and the online loop, including shadow or canary and sampled scoring
Names failure modes with detection, plus metrics and a rollout order
States flip conditions and labels preview features with a fallback

followUps.q: The judge agrees with your expert 92% of the time. Do you trust it?
followUps.a: Not yet. With imbalanced classes raw agreement can hide a judge that misses most failures, so check true positive and true negative rates. Swap order for pairwise, test on a fresh sample and recalibrate whenever the judge model changes.

followUps.q: Your gate score moved from 4.2 to 4.4. Do you ship?
followUps.a: Not on that alone. Without an interval, a paired comparison and a calibrated scale it is probably noise. At 100 tasks and an 80% pass rate the 95% half-width is about 7.8 points. Use a baseline comparison with a significance test, more trials or a larger set.

followUps.q: There are no traces and launch is in two weeks. What do you build first?
followUps.a: Twenty to fifty hand-written cases from known failure types, a reviewed synthetic batch from the agent definition and documents, component evals for retrieval and tools, a calibrated pass/fail judge and a held-out slice. Then a soft launch with sampled scoring so real traces start feeding the set.

redFlags: Names a tool or metric before asking about risk, stages and labels
Treats a single judge score as ground truth with no calibration or interval
Uses faithfulness alone and calls the answer correct
Lets one run decide a release with non-deterministic output

takeaways: Open with the dials: harm, stages, labels, traffic, expert time, budget and rollback speed.
Layer the checks: component, end-to-end, gate, red team, shadow and sampled live scoring.
Say how you calibrate the judge and how you quantify noise.
Close with failure modes, metrics, rollout order and what would flip your plan.
